text: About 150 years ago in France, an art academy liked smooth, careful paintings of history, religion and important people.
When its judges turned many paintings away, Emperor Napoleon III let the public see them at a show of their own.
src: 1874 to 1886 / the Académie des Beaux-Arts dominated French art. It valued historical subjects, religious themes and portraits over landscape and still life, and preferred carefully finished pictures
In 1863 it rejected Manet’s Le déjeuner sur l’herbe, and Emperor Napoleon III let the public judge the rejected works at a Salon des Refusés

text: New things helped young painters: paint in tin tubes, bright new colours, and Japanese prints with unusual angles.
src: Premixed paints in tin tubes, introduced in the mid-century, let artists work more spontaneously, and vivid synthetic pigments such as cobalt blue, viridian and cadmium yellow had become available / Japanese ukiyo-e prints, with their unusual angles

text: Shut out by the judges, the painters held their own shows, the first in the studio of a photographer named Nadar.
Women painters such as Berthe Morisot and Mary Cassatt took part, though they faced heavy limits.
src: Shut out by the Salon jury, they founded their own society in December 1873 and held eight independent exhibitions from 1874 to 1886 / in April 1874 in the studio of the photographer Nadar
Women took part under heavy limits / Mary Cassatt, Eva Gonzalès, Marie Bracquemond and Berthe Morisot were known as the “Women Impressionists”

text: They painted outdoors to catch the passing sunlight, with short strokes of pure colour side by side.
A critic made fun of Claude Monet’s painting Impression, Sunrise, and the name “Impressionists” stuck.
src: Impressionist painters worked in the open air to catch the passing effects of sunlight, laying short, broken strokes of pure colour side by side
the critic Louis Leroy played on the title of Claude Monet’s Impression, Sunrise / the name was soon taken up by the public and the artists

text: At first many people attacked their work, but slowly the public came to see it as fresh and new.
It opened the way for later painters like Vincent van Gogh, and spread as far as America, Australia and Japan.
src: The Impressionists faced harsh opposition from the conventional art community in France / Yet the public, at first hostile, gradually came to believe that they had captured a fresh and original vision
the movement became a precursor of Post-Impressionism / Vincent van Gogh / later shown in London and New York and taken up across Europe, the Americas, Australia and Japan
